title: the Mandukya Karika (Gaudapada)
hook: one blade of grass, dipped in the sea, one drop at a time, until the sea is empty. Gaudapada uses that picture for steadying the mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Karika and ajati, no birth: no one bound, no one freed. Did a worry tell you when it was born? Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

One blade of grass. Dip its tip in the sea. Lift it. One drop hangs there, shining, and falls onto the sand. Dip it again. Another drop. Now keep going, without hurry and without giving up, until the sea is empty. It sounds like a riddle, or a punishment from an old story. It's neither. It's a line from the Mandukya Karika, and Gaudapada isn't joking. He's describing how to steady a mind, and he says it takes exactly that kind of patience. After so much talk of no birth and ropes in the dark, today: his practical verses.
screen: `A BLADE OF GRASS, THE SEA.` → `ONE DROP AT A TIME.` → `THE PATIENCE OF STEADYING A MIND.`

segments.voice: It would be easy to think Gaudapada has nothing to say about practice. He does. He names a discipline asparsha yoga, the yoga of no contact, meaning no grasping, no clinging to what appears. And he admits it's hard. Even yogis, he says, are afraid of it. They see fear where there's nothing to fear. Then comes the image. The mind is to be steadied without growing weary, the way someone might empty the ocean drop by drop with the tip of a blade of grass. The point isn't that the task can be finished by Tuesday. It's the kind of effort: tireless, unhurried, and not discouraged. Then he gets specific, almost like a coach. When the mind drifts toward dullness and sleep, wake it. When it's scattered, bring it back to calm. When it's caught in desire, know that it's caught. When it's resting in balance, don't disturb it. And one more warning that surprises some readers: don't sit and savor the happiness that comes in deep stillness. Stay unattached, through clear seeing. Even the sweet part isn't something to grab. This fits the rest of the Karika. If nothing is truly born, the practice isn't building something new. It's the steady, patient undoing of grasping, until the mind, in his words elsewhere, stops imagining and comes to rest. Other traditions of meditation in India have their own instructions. These are Gaudapada's, and they're humble ones: wake it, calm it, notice it, leave it be.
screen: `ASPARSHA: THE YOGA OF NO CONTACT.` · `THE OCEAN AND A BLADE OF GRASS.` · `WAKE IT, CALM IT, NOTICE, LEAVE IT.` · `DON'T SAVOR EVEN THE STILLNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: Gaudapada's four small moves. Settle, and breathe. If the mind gets drowsy, sit up a little and open your attention. If it scatters, come back to one breath. If it reaches for something, a plan or a craving, just notice: caught. And if it rests, let it rest, without holding on to the rest. One drop at a time, like the blade of grass. If you pray, you can let each return be an offering. The bell holds the time.
The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, with their patient practice: steadying the mind like emptying the ocean with a blade of grass. Today's word.
Your line: the Mandukya Karika, Gaudapada. Today, when your attention drifts yet again, bring it back as calmly as the first time. Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, meditation is practiced alongside study and reflection, and Gaudapada's verses on steadying the mind are read as guidance for it.

original.note: Sanskrit: no contact, no touching; Gaudapada's name for his yoga of non-grasping.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Karika is all theory, with nothing to practice.
what it means: Gaudapada teaches a patient yoga of no grasping: wake the mind, calm it, notice it, leave it be.
what a scholar hears: Mandukya Karika 3.39–3.46, asparsha yoga, the ocean emptied with the tip of a kusha blade, and the warning against savoring the bliss.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

sources.ref: Mandukya Karika 3.39 (asparsha yoga, hard to see; yogis afraid of it, seeing fear in the fearless)
Mandukya Karika 3.41 (the mind restrained without weariness, like emptying the ocean drop by drop with the tip of a blade of kusha grass)
Mandukya Karika 3.42–3.46 (wake the mind in torpor, calm it when scattered, know it when caught in desire, do not disturb it in balance, do not savor the bliss, be unattached through discernment)

notes: Confirm verse references and paraphrases for Karika 3.39–3.46: asparsha yoga; yogis' fear; the ocean emptied drop by drop with a kusha blade (3.41); the instructions for laya (torpor), vikshepa (distraction), kashaya (latent desire), and samaprapta (balance); not savoring the bliss (3.45).
'Until the mind stops imagining and comes to rest' alludes to Karika 3.31–3.32 (the mind that does not imagine becomes no-mind); attributed as 'his words elsewhere'. Confirm.
'Other traditions of meditation in India have their own instructions' is neutral and does not compare; confirm.
